title: [Chapitre] VI. Analysis situs (deuxième mouture) : notes manuscrites (18-20/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Context: in the 1986 'Analysis situs (deuxième mouture)' notes, Grothendieck sets up a combinatorial-set-theoretic framework of 'ateliers' (workshops). An atelier is a set L of points together with a family 𝓕 of admissible 'figures' in L. Here a figure is a configuration built from 'elementary figures' (multistrates), partially ordered by the sub-figure relation ≤. Two figures can be joined (F ∨ G) when they are multistratum-wise compatible. On p.55 he listed axioms for a subset 𝓕 ⊂ Fig(L):
- Axiom*2: 𝓕 is closed downward under ≤.
- Axiom*3: if F, G ∈ 𝓕 and every pair of multistrates F_A, G_B is compatible, with {F_A, G_B} a joint in 𝓕, then F ∨ G ∈ 𝓕.
He then began re-expressing this through a set 𝓜 of elementary figures with a reflexive, symmetric 'geometric compatibility' relation, subject to:
- 𝓜1: every point {{x}} lies in 𝓜.
- 𝓜2: 𝓜 is closed under sub-multistrates.
- 𝓜3: compatibility is inherited by sub-multistrates and implies the ambient compatibility.

This page states the resulting 'Scholie' for (special/general) set-theoretic ateliers generated by figures of finite type. Giving such an atelier is equivalent to giving a pair (L, 𝓜) such that:
- L is a set;
- 𝓜 is a set of elementary figures in L;
- every sub-figure of an X ∈ 𝓜 is of finite type (automatic if the X ∈ 𝓜 are finite figures);
- Axioms 𝓜1–𝓜3 hold.
Conversely, 𝓕 is reconstructed as the sub-atelier of Fig(L) consisting of the set-theoretic figures of finite type all of whose multistrates lie in 𝓜.

In modern terms, this is a generators-and-relations description. A downward-closed family that is closed under pairwise-compatible joins is determined by its 'atoms' (the elementary figures) plus a hereditary reflexive-symmetric compatibility relation. Admissible figures are then the finite 'cliques' of compatible atoms, exactly as a flag (clique) complex is determined by its 1-skeleton. The same structure underlies a coherence space or binary-coherent stable domain.

The last paragraph raises a further question: for a figure F whose multistrates all lie in 𝓜, does membership in 𝓕 depend only on its 'ombre' (shadow, presumably its underlying point-set or support)? The next page answers that one should not expect 𝓕 to be closed under arbitrary limits ('spécial'), only 'finitely special'. Via the atomicity axiom 3, that condition reduces to the compatibility relation on 𝓜 being the set-theoretic one, leading to a corollary classifying finitely special set-theoretic ateliers by pairs (L, 𝓜).

Purpose: to give a finitary, combinatorial presentation of the 'ateliers' that serve as models of tame/stratified spaces in his analysis situs programme.
errors: No mathematical error is visible, but the Scholie is stated without proof.
The precise meaning of 'figure de type fini', 'multistrate' and 'ombre' depends on definitions on earlier pages, so the equivalence cannot be fully checked from this page alone.

The page leaves implicit that the reconstructed 𝓕 must also require pairwise compatibility of the multistrates of a figure (Axiom 𝓜3). Without that requirement, 'all multistrates in 𝓜' would not reproduce Axiom*3.

ideas.what: Equivalence between set-theoretic ateliers of finite type and pairs (L, 𝓜): a set of elementary figures closed under sub-objects with a hereditary reflexive-symmetric compatibility relation. 𝓕 is recovered as the finite-type figures whose multistrates all lie in 𝓜.
ideas.modern_name: Presentation of a downward-closed, pairwise-join-closed family by atoms plus a compatibility relation (flag/clique complex; coherence space / binary-coherent stable domain)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Flag complexes: combinatorial folklore. Coherence spaces: Girard (1986–87). Stable/coherent domains: Berry (1978), Plotkin.
ideas.where_published: Unpublished; the 'ateliers' framework of Analysis situs 1986 is not in his circulated texts as far as known.

ideas.what: Question whether membership of a figure in 𝓕 depends only on its 'ombre' (underlying support). This leads on the next page to the notion of 'finitely special' ateliers, characterised by the compatibility relation being the set-theoretic one.

missed.claim: The axioms (downward closure plus 'pairwise compatible ⇒ join exists in 𝓕', with 𝓕 generated by atoms under a reflexive symmetric compatibility relation) are essentially the axioms of Girard's coherence spaces / binary-coherent stable domains and of flag complexes. Grothendieck wrote this in June 1986, contemporaneously with and independently of Girard, in a topological-combinatorial setting. The link between his 'ateliers' for tame topology and coherence-space semantics has not been noted.
missed.quote: se donner un couple (L, M), L ensemble, M ens. de figures élémentaires dans L ... On reconstitue 𝓕 comme un sous-atelier de Fig(L), formé des figures ens. de type fini telles que ses multistrates soient dans M.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is mainly of historical interest. It shows Grothendieck's late 'ateliers' formalism is a stratified enrichment of a well-understood structure (cliques of a coherence relation). That would make his unpublished Analysis situs notes easier to formalise and compare with domain theory and combinatorial topology.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a technical bookkeeping step in an unpublished framework (ateliers) that is itself little known. The Scholie is a natural generators-and-relations reformulation. Its resemblance to coherence spaces and flag complexes is a mild curiosity, not a new result.
transcription_corrections: 'Axiom H1 – Axiom H3' should read 'Axiome 𝓜1 – Axiome 𝓜3', referring to the axioms on p.55.
'd'un x ∈ M' / 'les x ∈ M' should read uppercase 'X ∈ 𝓜' (elements of 𝓜 are figures, not points).
The superscript after 'ateliers' reads more like '(spéciaux)' than '(génér.)'; compare 'ateliers (spéciaux) ensemblistes' on p.57.
The struck-out passage at the bottom is likely '[on pourrait s'attendre à ce que pour une]' rather than '[se demander que pour une]'.
'M' should be the script set 𝓜 throughout, consistent with p.55.
